title: Singles: Discerning Before Committing
subtitle: 28 days of prayer in the light of the Bible and under the guidance of the Holy Spirit
movements: Getting to Know the Other Person Truthfully
intro:
You desire to marry and are wondering how to discern a relationship. Perhaps you have received several proposals, several people interest you, or a relationship already exists. Perhaps you have no one particular in mind. You can bring each of these situations to God with confidence.

The question at the heart of this journey is: "Lord, in the light of your Word and under the guidance of your Spirit, help me to discern this relationship and to choose with wisdom, truth, and love."

The Bible is our authority. The Holy Spirit illuminates us, corrects us, and leads us; we seek his direction through prayer and obedience. Our impressions and understanding, however, need to be tested. A personal conviction is not sufficient to commit another person to marriage.

This journey helps you discern a next step. The 28 days set no deadline for choosing a spouse. A relationship takes time to truly know. Your singleness diminishes neither your worth before God nor your place in the Church.

A simple rhythm

Set aside approximately 15 to 20 minutes to read, reflect, pray, and write. The suggested actions may require a separate time: a conversation should not be rushed in order to finish a day. You may revisit a day or extend a week. External resources are optional and supplement this time.

Read the passages in your Bible. The reflections, prayers, and questions that follow are companion texts, never new words of Scripture. The prayers are suggestions to personalize. The time of listening does not require any particular feeling or message to be received.

In your personal journal, distinguish between observed facts, feelings, interpretations or impressions that need to be tested, and questions that remain open.

Your notes belong to you. You may use initials and share only a chosen summary with a trusted person. No one needs access to your journal to prove that you are sincere.

Adapting the days to your situation

- Several proposals received: you may ask for time, decline a proposal, or choose not to pursue any possibility. A declaration creates no obligation.
- Several people of interest: distinguish between interest and an actual relationship. Respect each person and clarify your intentions without making incompatible promises.
- An ongoing relationship: examine your mutual desire to continue; the suggested conversations assume that each person is free to speak openly.
- No one particular in mind: work on your expectations, your character, and your current relationships. You do not need to invent a candidate in order to move forward.

These situations may apply to women and men alike. The same requirements of truth, respect, and self-control apply to everyone.

From the outset: control, humiliation, threats, and sexual or spiritual pressure must not be minimized. If a situation puts you in danger, seek safe support without waiting for day 25. Prayer and forgiveness do not obligate you to expose yourself to violence. The conversation steps in this journal are optional and must be adapted to your safety.
biblical: The Bible is our authority. We seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit through prayer and obedience, testing our impressions and our understanding. James invites believers going through trials to ask for God's wisdom. This journey applies that invitation to the discernment of a relationship, without turning this passage into a method for obtaining the name of a spouse. The reflections explain the context of the texts and distinguish their meaning from their application to a romantic relationship.
completion: You have devoted 28 days to the Word, to prayer, and to a truer knowledge of yourself and your relationships. Thank God for what you have learned. You may continue getting to know each other mutually, consider marriage preparation together, wait or take a pause to seek clarity, or step back from a relationship. Every shared step requires free and mutual consent. The end of the journey sets no deadline for choosing a spouse. If no relationship is in view, continue your life with God, your friendships, and your responsibilities. Your singleness diminishes neither your worth nor your place in the Church.

labels.planDiscernmentReview: My review and my next step

days.theme: Lord, give me wisdom to discern
days.reflection:
James writes to believers facing trials. He invites them to persevere and to ask God for the wisdom they lack. This passage does not provide a method for obtaining the name of a spouse; it teaches us to turn to God in the midst of our difficulties.

In romantic discernment, this wisdom begins with recognizing our limitations. A genuine attraction may come before we know the other person sufficiently. The urge to decide quickly may stem from a fear of missing an opportunity. Asking God to enlighten us means accepting that a conversation, an observation, or a correction can change the way we see things.

Trusting God does not mean you must already be certain of your choice. Being torn between people is not, in itself, a lack of faith. You can bring your questions to Him without demanding that all of them find their answer today.
days.practice: Identify one piece of information you are missing and one respectful way to obtain it. If there is no specific person in mind, write down one expectation about marriage that you wish to examine before God.

discernment.reading: Observe the situation of the believers, the way in which God gives, and the attitude of trust to which James calls them.
discernment.prayer: Father, I come to You with my desire to love and to build a home. You know my hopes and my attachments. I acknowledge that fear, appearances, or the need to be chosen can influence how I see things. Give me Your wisdom. Forgive me when I seek only to have my own preferences confirmed. Holy Spirit, enlighten my understanding through the Word and make my heart open to Your guidance. Teach me to respect every person involved. Keep me from premature promises and give me the courage to ask the questions that need to be asked. May my desire for marriage remain submitted to You. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Read the passage again in quietness. Ask: "Holy Spirit, help me to recognize what I need to understand and to put into practice today." Note an attitude, a question, or a course of action. If an impression arises, record it as such and allow it to be tested.
questions: What do I hope to receive from this journey?
What outcome am I most afraid to consider, and why?
What fact do I tend to minimize because it conflicts with my desire?
discernment.deeper: Return to the passage on wisdom offered as supplementary reading.

days.theme: Welcoming the authority of the Word
days.reflection:
Paul encourages Timothy to remain in what he has received. The Scriptures lead him to wisdom for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ and equip him to act rightly. They also teach by rebuking and correcting.

In a relationship, we may look for passages that reassure our preference and avoid those that challenge our conduct. Welcoming the authority of the Bible means allowing it to examine our manner of speaking, of desiring, of making promises, and of treating the other person as well.

An isolated verse should not bear a conclusion that its context does not support. A marriage story in the Bible is not automatically a blueprint for every single person. Read what comes before and after; distinguish between commandment, narrative, and the application you are proposing. God is not asking you to make the text say the name of the person you hope to marry.
days.practice: Choose a verse you often use in your reflections on love and read its entire paragraph. Write down its primary meaning before recording your personal application.

discernment.reading: Observe what the Scriptures bring to Timothy and the kind of life toward which they are shaping him.
discernment.prayer: Lord, thank You for Your Word that teaches and forms me. Deliver me from the habit of holding on only to what suits me. Grant me the grace to receive with trust what corrects me. Holy Spirit, help me to understand the Scriptures and to obey them in my relational life. Teach me to recognize the difference between what the text actually says and what I would like it to say. May my choices reflect my devotion to Jesus. Amen.
discernment.listening: Return to one clear teaching from the passage. What place could you give it today? You may seek help in understanding a text without waiting until you have mastered everything before you pray.
questions: Which conviction about marriage genuinely comes from a passage understood in its context?
Which expectation comes more from my community, my family, or a personal experience?
In what area is the Word already inviting me to change?
discernment.deeper: Continue with the supplementary biblical reading and reflect on how to put it into practice.

days.theme: Letting Myself Be Led by the Holy Spirit
days.reflection:
Paul describes a life transformed by the Spirit and the assurance of belonging to God as his children. Being led by the Spirit concerns our entire walk with God. In this passage, it is not a code for deciphering every particular decision.

You can nonetheless genuinely seek his guidance for a relationship: asking him to enlighten you, correct your motivations, and help you recognize the right step. This openness is also lived out in what is already clear: renouncing deception, respecting a refusal, keeping your word, or asking for forgiveness.

Sometimes we wait for an extraordinary sign while putting off a simple act of obedience. Moving forward with the Spirit also means welcoming this daily transformation. You do not have to manufacture an emotion or an inner voice to prove that he is present. Approach the Father as his child, with your questions and with confidence.
days.practice: Put one already-clear thing into practice: correct something you said, honor a boundary, or return to a time of reading and prayer.

discernment.reading: Observe the connection between being led by the Spirit, the struggle against sin, and our relationship with the Father.
discernment.prayer: Father, thank you for receiving me in Jesus. Holy Spirit, lead me in truth and grow within me a life that is pleasing to God. I bring this relationship and the choices that lie ahead of me before you. Correct whatever is drawing me away from you, shed light on what I misunderstand, and strengthen what is right. Give me the courage to obey what you have already made clear to me. May my longing for an answer never cause me to neglect my communion with you. Amen.
discernment.listening: Stay for a moment before God with this question: 'What attitude do I need to surrender to you?' Return to the passage and freely note what it brings to light, without attributing to it a certainty it does not give.
questions: How do I usually seek the Spirit's guidance?
What simple act of obedience have I been putting off?
What difference does being loved by the Father make to my need to be chosen?
discernment.deeper: Reread the entire chapter to keep the context. The supplementary reading connects walking by the Spirit to everyday conduct.

days.theme: Bringing My Desires and Motivations Before God
days.reflection:
The psalmist addresses a God who knows him deeply and asks him to examine his life. This prayer can help us move beyond the desire to appear blameless. God knows our desires before we find the words to name them.

The desire for marriage can intertwine the longing to love, to share faith, to build a home, the fear of loneliness, and the need to reassure those around us. Acknowledging this mixture opens a path of honesty. It does not make your desire illegitimate.

Also ask yourself whether you are looking at a person for who they are or primarily for what they might resolve in your life. A spouse cannot bear full responsibility for your identity and your sense of peace. Entrust your needs to God and welcome the forms of support, friendship, and growth that are already available to you. You can learn to love without waiting until you have become a person with no vulnerabilities.
days.practice: Complete two sentences: 'I desire to marry because…' and 'I am afraid of remaining single because…'. Reread them without condemning yourself.

discernment.reading: , then reread verses 1–6. Observe how the final request flows from the knowledge God already has of the psalmist.
discernment.prayer: Lord, you know my heart. I entrust to you my desire for tenderness, companionship, and commitment. Show me the expectations I find it hard to acknowledge. Forgive me if I reduce someone to the role they might play in my life. Holy Spirit, work on my motivations and teach me to love with honesty. Help me to receive the friendship and support I need today. Guide my desires so that they find their rightful place before you. Amen.
discernment.listening: Simply name one desire and one fear. Bring them before God without immediately correcting them. Then ask what a faithful response to them might look like for you today.
questions: What draws me to marriage, beyond the ceremony and the status it brings?
What am I expecting from another person that no one could ever guarantee?
What need can I already entrust to God and share with a trustworthy person?
discernment.deeper: Psalm 62:6–9. Return to your notes from day 1.

days.theme: Honoring My Life as a Single Person
days.reflection:
Paul considers both marriage and singleness before God. He highlights the opportunities for availability to the Lord and explains that he seeks the good of those he is addressing, without laying a trap for them. His counsel also takes their situation into account.

This passage prevents us from viewing singleness as an incomplete Christian life. Your service, your friendships, and your belonging to the Church have value right now. Marriage is a commitment to discern, not a spiritual promotion to be earned.

You can receive this even while feeling the pain of an unmet desire. Expressing that pain does not make you ungrateful. Nor do you need to conclude today that you will remain single for the rest of your life. Live your present situation before God, keeping your desire open and your relationships alive. Personal growth is not a means of making God indebted to you in the matter of marriage.
days.practice: Set aside time for a friendship, a commitment, or a project that has value today, without turning it into a strategy for meeting someone.

discernment.reading: If possible, also read through verses 25–31 to place Paul's counsel in context.
discernment.prayer: Father, I thank You for the life You are giving me today. I also entrust to You the expectations that cause me pain. Free me from comparison and from the idea that my worth depends on a romantic commitment. Holy Spirit, teach me to serve, to love, and to receive love in my current situation. I place my desire for marriage in Your hands. Keep my hope anchored in You, and show me the relationships I can cultivate now. Amen.
discernment.listening: Bring to mind a relationship, a gift you have received, or an opportunity for service for which you can thank God. Also leave honest room for what remains painful.
questions: In what situations do I feel I have to justify my singleness?
What present joy or responsibility am I postponing until 'when I am married'?
Who helps me feel like a full member of the community?
discernment.deeper: Reread the entire chapter, holding together the teachings on both singleness and marriage.

days.theme: Entrusting My Worries and the Pressures I Feel
days.reflection:
Paul invites believers to bring their needs before God and to direct their minds toward what is true and right. The peace of God accompanies a life turned toward Him. The text does not make this peace a signal that certifies a particular person is the right spouse.

Age, remarks from family, or the fear that an opportunity will disappear can create an inner sense of urgency. These pressures deserve to be named. Their intensity is not, in itself, a sufficient reason to commit. Conversely, feeling anxious does not prove that God is withholding a relationship.

You can pray while also taking simple practical steps: asking for more time, limiting certain repetitive conversations, and making yourself available for an important discussion. If anxiety is overwhelming your life, seeking appropriate support is compatible with trusting God. You do not need to deny how you feel in order to come before Him.
days.practice: Prepare a simple sentence: "Thank you for caring about me. I need time to discern, and I will share my decision with you when I am ready." Adapt it to your situation.

discernment.reading: Notice the place of prayer, thanksgiving, attentiveness, and putting things into practice.
discernment.prayer: Lord, here is what worries me and what I am afraid of losing. I entrust to You the words that pressure me and the comparisons that wear me out. Thank You for receiving me with all my needs. Holy Spirit, help me to recognize what is true and not to make decisions driven solely by fear. Grant me Your peace and the freedom to ask for the time I need. Teach me to set boundaries with respect and to receive help. Amen.
discernment.listening: Bring a specific worry before God. After a moment of silence, write down what falls within the realm of a possible step forward and what lies outside your control. You do not have to produce a sense of calm before continuing with your day.
questions: Who or what makes me feel I must choose quickly?
What is the difference between a real constraint and an anticipated fear?
What kind of help do I need in order to regain space for reflection?
discernment.deeper: Matthew 6:25–34. Note what Jesus invites us to seek today, without turning this passage into a guarantee of future marriage.

days.theme: Review: Am I open to being redirected?
days.reflection:
The psalmist asks to be taught and guided. He presents not merely an outcome to be achieved, but his own walk to be led. This posture gives meaning to our first week.

Reviewing is not about checking whether you have prayed well enough to deserve an answer. Look instead at what is becoming more true: a desire more clearly named, a pressure acknowledged, an expectation put back in its proper place, or an obedience begun. A modest realization can already make your perspective more accurate.

You can still prefer a particular outcome while remaining open before God. What matters is not ruling out in advance everything that might contradict it. A correction may concern your pace, your way of getting to know the other person, or the relationship itself. No review obliges you to make a decision today. Make room for gratitude and for the next step of learning.
days.practice: Write a three-line review: one thing to be grateful for, one expectation to entrust to God, one step to continue. If you wish, share only these three lines with a trusted person.

discernment.reading: , then verses 8–10. Notice what the psalmist asks God to teach him.
discernment.prayer: Father, thank you for what you have allowed me to understand this week. I bring you my progress and my resistance. Holy Spirit, keep my heart teachable. If I am clinging to a conclusion before knowing the reality, help me to loosen my grip. If fear is closing me off from any relationship, lead me gently. Grant me the grace to keep seeking you with confidence and to act on what has become clear. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Reread a note that stood out to you. Bring it before God, then remain for a moment in gratitude. Do not treat the repetition of a thought as automatic proof of its divine origin.
questions: What have I learned about my motivations, my fears, and my expectations?
On what point am I willing to be corrected or redirected?
What question will I keep open for the coming week?
discernment.deeper: Return to the passage from this week that still calls for your attention. The same text can be meditated on for several days.

days.reflection:
The creation narrative presents the union of man and woman in a relationship that encompasses their whole lives. It calls us to take marriage seriously: it is about building a communion and a faithfulness that goes beyond the joy of early days or the success of a ceremony.

This passage does not explain how to identify, among several people, a spouse designated by some secret sign. The meeting of Adam and Eve belongs to the creation narrative; its circumstances do not constitute a method for finding a spouse. The Bible also affirms the value of singleness, as we saw on day 5.

Ask yourself today what you genuinely want to share: decisions, responsibilities, a life of faith, joys and difficulties. Another person is not an answer to all your needs. Preparing for commitment involves learning to give and to receive, to speak truthfully, and to respect the other person's freedom. A plan for marriage must be something both people can want and express together.
days.practice: Complete these two sentences in your own words: "In marriage, I want to build…" and "In order to contribute to that, I need to grow in…" If a relationship exists, keep these notes for a conversation at the appropriate time.

discernment.reading: Notice what the narrative says about relationship, attachment, and shared life.
discernment.prayer: Lord, form in me a right vision of marriage. Teach me to desire a shared life marked by faithfulness, and not merely the relief of being chosen. Holy Spirit, shed light on the expectations I need to deepen or correct. Prepare me to take on my responsibilities and to receive the other person as a whole person, with their freedom, their history, and their limitations. May my desire for commitment remain subject to your Word. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Bring before God the image of marriage you have carried since childhood. Allow what deserves to be examined to rise to the surface. You can acknowledge a family influence without condemning your entire history.
questions: What does marriage represent to me, beyond the ceremony?
What responsibility am I ready to take on, and which one concerns me?
What expectation do I need to bring into dialogue with Scripture and with reality?
discernment.deeper: Read Matthew 19:3–6: Jesus responds to a question about divorce by recalling the seriousness of the union. This passage does not provide a procedure for selecting a spouse.

days.reflection:
Paul describes love in the middle of a teaching about the life of the Church. This passage therefore concerns all Christian relationships. Applying it to a romantic relationship is legitimate, but it was not written as a checklist for certifying a future marriage.

Attraction can be a beautiful beginning. On its own, it does not reveal how two people will treat each other over time. Pay attention to the room left for listening, for truth, for respecting a refusal, and for rejoicing in the other person's good. Ask these questions of your own conduct as well: loving is not simply a matter of waiting for qualities to appear in someone else.

You do not have to manufacture attraction toward someone whose qualities you recognize. Nor do you have to call love a relationship that humiliates you. Christian patience does not require enduring violence; this very passage connects love to the refusal of injustice. Discernment allows you to recognize what is genuinely being built, without idealizing an emotion or reducing the other person to their faults.
days.practice: Offer a gesture of attention without seeking a romantic response in return. In an existing relationship, observe ordinary situations; do not arrange a test to try the other person.

discernment.reading: Place these verses in their context between chapters 12 and 14, which are devoted in particular to spiritual gifts and the life of the community.
discernment.prayer: Jesus, teach me to love in truth. Thank you for the capacity to feel affection and to rejoice in an encounter. Holy Spirit, grow in me a love that is patient and attentive, free from possessiveness and contempt. Open my eyes to the way I treat others. Grant me also the clarity I need so as not to confuse the intensity of a feeling with the quality of a relationship. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Think of a recent interaction. Bring it before God without rewriting what happened. What attitude of love can you choose right now, even if this relationship never becomes a romantic one?
questions: What attracts me, and what do I actually know about this person?
What concrete act of respect or attention have I observed or offered?
Where is attraction leading me to minimize a difficulty?
discernment.deeper: Read 1 John 3:16–18 on a love that expresses itself in actions and in sharing.

days.theme: Watching the Fruit as It Ripens
days.reflection:
Paul is addressing believers called to walk by the Spirit. The fruit he describes is not a talent reserved for a few people. It touches the way of living, desiring, and entering into relationship.

In romantic discernment, eloquent speech, a role in the Church, or an impressive spiritual experience are not enough to know someone's character. Look at what manifests over time: how does this person receive a frustration, share attention, acknowledge their faults, respect boundaries? A single observation does not tell the whole story of a life; repeated behaviors nevertheless deserve to be taken seriously.

This same gaze applies to you. This journey does not place you above the other person in the role of examiner. Ask the Holy Spirit to mature your own character. You can acknowledge genuine growth without demanding perfection. A request for forgiveness becomes credible when it is accompanied by assumed responsibility and consistent actions over time; it does not obligate you to continue a relationship.
days.practice: Choose one specific habit to work on this week: letting someone finish a sentence, honoring a boundary, acknowledging a fault, or keeping a commitment. Note what you actually practiced.

discernment.reading: Observe how Paul connects the work of the Spirit to everyday conduct.
discernment.prayer: Holy Spirit, bear fruit in my life. Work patience, gentleness, and self-control into me in the situations where I most easily lose them. Keep me from judging by appearances or by spiritual prestige. Give me the ability to recognize sincere growth and to honestly name what repeats itself without changing. May I remain open to your work in my own heart. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Read slowly through the qualities Paul mentions. Pause on just one of them and ask God how to practice it today. You do not need to measure your entire maturity in a few minutes.
questions: In what situation do I most need to grow?
What behaviors have I observed more than once, and in what context?
Have I confused spiritual ease, reputation, or success with maturity?
discernment.deeper: Reread Galatians 5:13–15 to situate this conduct within the call to serve others in love.

days.reflection:
James challenges a profession of faith that remains silent in the face of a brother's or sister's needs. He calls for consistency between what is declared and what is lived. The passage does not teach that one must be wealthy, highly active, or socially confident in order to have genuine faith.

In a relationship, shared faith is also revealed outside of religious conversations. How does each person treat someone who can offer them nothing? What place do they give to compassion, justice, and quiet service? A reserved person may live a deep faith; a highly visible person may still have much to learn. The resources available, the health, and the responsibilities of each person must be considered fairly.

Look at these things with humility. You do not know everything the other person does in secret, and you are not called to pronounce a verdict on their salvation. You can, however, ask whether your relationship encourages sincere faith and concrete obedience. Begin by letting the Word examine your own way of loving.
days.practice: Perform an accessible act of service without staging it to impress anyone. If you are thinking about a particular person, remain attentive to natural opportunities to get to know their life.

discernment.reading: Notice the concrete, material example James chooses to speak about faith.
discernment.prayer: Father, may my faith take shape in my life. Forgive me for generous words that are accompanied by no real attention. Holy Spirit, make me sensitive to the needs I can meet with the resources I have. Teach me to know the other person rightly, without being dazzled by their visibility or dismissive of their quietness. Lead me toward relationships where faith and action go hand in hand. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Ask God to make you attentive to a person or a responsibility you have been neglecting. Examine what comes to mind, then choose a response proportionate to your situation.
questions: Where is my faith already expressing itself in my everyday actions?
What do I know about how the other person treats vulnerable people?
What conclusion have I drawn too quickly based on someone's reputation?
discernment.deeper: Read James 2:1–9: the prohibition of favoritism also sheds light on our tendency to privilege status and appearance.

days.reflection:
Paul connects new life to specific actions: speaking truthfully, taking responsibility for one's conduct, and acting honestly. This ethic applies to all believers. In a romantic relationship, it helps lay the foundations of trust.

Being reliable does not mean having a good income, a degree, or a life without difficulties. A person may be going through a period of unemployment while still being responsible and sincere. Another may have an impressive situation and yet be prone to dishonesty. Look at the relationship between commitments made, actions taken, and the way a person acknowledges falling short.

Transparency is built according to the depth of the relationship. It does not give anyone the right to control the other person's accounts, passwords, or all of their private communications. However, a plan for marriage does call for honest conversations about commitments and realities that will affect shared life. It is possible to respect someone's privacy while refusing to accept a misleading presentation of oneself. Receiving a difficult truth allows you to reflect on a real basis; it does not obligate you to accept everything.
days.practice: Honor a specific commitment or clearly correct an inaccurate statement. For a question concerning the other person, prepare a respectful inquiry rather than a covert check.

discernment.reading: Observe the concrete changes asked of members of the community.
discernment.prayer: God of truth, teach me to speak plainly and to keep my word. If I have exaggerated, hidden something important, or promised too quickly, give me the courage to make it right. Holy Spirit, free me from the need to appear a certain way and from the temptation to control. Help me to build trust through honest actions, to acknowledge my limitations, and to respect those of the other person. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Bring a recent commitment before God. Do you need to honor it, clarify its limits, or acknowledge that you will not be able to keep it? Receive this responsibility without constructing a spiritual excuse.
questions: What facts form the basis of my current trust?
How does each person respond when a promise has not been kept?
What honest conversation would be appropriate for the current stage of the relationship?
discernment.deeper: Read Proverbs 12:17–22 on truth and the effect of words.

days.reflection:
These passages teach a way of living together under God's authority. They do not assume that believers will always be of the same mind. They raise the question of what we do with our differences and our emotions.

A disagreement can reveal the capacity to listen, to restate what has been said, and to seek a solution. It can also expose a refusal to take any responsibility. Notice whether each person can speak without being humiliated, set a boundary, and ask for a pause. A calm temperament does not guarantee respect; visible emotion does not cancel the legitimacy of what is being expressed. It is the actions themselves, their context, and their repetition that must be examined.

Reconciliation requires more than a formulaic apology. Can the wrong be named, can what is repairable be repaired, and can behavior actually change? A quarrel never justifies threats or violence. If you are afraid of the other person's reactions, you may seek individual support before any conversation takes place. The approach proposed today concerns an exchange in which each person has the freedom to speak and to stop.
days.practice: In a safe exchange, restate what you have understood before you respond. If tension rises, suggest a pause and agree on a time to resume. If there is no current relationship, practice this kind of listening in a friendship.

discernment.reading: Observe the place given to listening, to words, and to the control of anger.
discernment.prayer: Lord, guard my mouth and open my ears. Help me to hear before I defend myself, to speak without putting others down, and to acknowledge my own share of responsibility. Holy Spirit, teach me to express disagreement with both firmness and respect. Where a relationship exists, grant us the willingness to learn and to repair. Shed light on whatever requires time, outside help, or a clear boundary. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Revisit a difficult exchange without immediately looking for who won. Ask God what depends on your own conduct. You are not required to take responsibility for the other person's actions.
questions: Can each person express disagreement without fearing punishment?
How have we addressed, or left unanswered, a recent wrong?
What listening habit do I need to practice?
discernment.deeper: The supplementary reading invites reflection on the way our words either soothe or wound.

days.theme: Taking Stock of What I Actually Know
days.reflection:
Proverbs shapes judgment through words of wisdom. Here, the impulse to answer without listening is called into question. Applied to a relationship, this principle invites us to make room for the facts that are still missing.

You may have known a person for a long time and yet not know how they envision marriage. You may also have met someone recently and feel a strong sense of closeness. Neither length of time alone nor intensity of feeling alone answers every question. Reread your notes: what have you actually observed, what have you heard directly, and what have you simply assumed?

This distinction does not require you to investigate the other person's private life. It helps you identify the conversations and ordinary situations that will allow you to know each other more fully. A difficulty does not disappear simply because it remains unexplained. An unknown area is not, however, a fault to be assigned. You can acknowledge what is good, name a concern, and leave a question open, without giving a person an overall verdict.
days.practice: Write down two dated examples with their context: one encouraging behavior and one point that needs clarification. If no one is currently involved, conduct this review of your own relational habits instead.

discernment.reading: Consider the call to listen before drawing conclusions.
discernment.prayer: Father, thank you for the people you allow me to meet and for what I learn through my relationships. Holy Spirit, strengthen my discernment. Help me to distinguish between what I know and what I hope. Keep me from hasty conclusions, from intrusive curiosity, and from a refusal to see clearly. Give me the patience to come to know others in truth and the courage to act when something is sufficiently clear. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Reread one encouraging observation and one question that is still open. Bring both to God without forcing either a favorable or an unfavorable conclusion. Ask for wisdom for the next step.
questions: What concrete fact confirmed or corrected my perception this week?
What hope have I been presenting as an already established reality?
What do I still need to know before considering a further step?
discernment.deeper: Read Proverbs 18:17, which cautions against mistaking a first account for a complete understanding.

days.reflection:
Verse 39 concerns a widow who is considering remarrying. Paul acknowledges her choice while placing it within the context of her belonging to the Lord. In this journey, we apply this guidance to the search for a marriage in which both people share faith in Christ. This application must be distinguished from the immediate recipient of the text. You may reread the entire chapter to keep it in context.

A shared faith deserves a concrete conversation. What place does each person give to Jesus, the Bible, prayer, and the life of the Church? How does each one wish to live out and pass on their faith? Two people who call themselves Christians may have very different expectations. Belonging to the same denomination does not automatically resolve these differences; different traditions call for an honest discussion of their implications.

Respect for every person remains essential, regardless of their faith. You do not need to provoke a religious declaration in order to obtain a commitment to marriage, nor should you promise marriage in exchange for a conversion. Faith cannot be imposed. Seek a sincere, free, and lived-out adherence, while recognizing that faith alone is not sufficient to establish that a commitment between you would be wise.
days.practice: Prepare two open-ended questions about lived faith. For example: "How do you want to make room for prayer in your life?" and "How do you envision passing on faith to children?" If you are not in a relationship, begin by answering these questions for yourself.

discernment.reading: Identify who Paul is directly addressing and the freedom he acknowledges.
discernment.prayer: Lord Jesus, I entrust the spiritual direction of my life to you. Teach me to take my faith seriously without using it to dominate or look down on others. Holy Spirit, grant me sincere conversations and the freedom to hear convictions different from my own. If a shared life is being considered, help us to look honestly at what we truly believe and what that involves. Keep us from any religious promise made only to preserve the relationship. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Present to God what is central to your faith. Ask him to help you express it simply, without organizing a biblical knowledge test for the other person.
questions: What concrete place does my faith occupy in my decisions?
What have we actually shared with each other about our spiritual life together?
What difference in conviction would need to be explored more deeply?
discernment.deeper: Read Ephesians 4:1–6 on unity, humility, and the way to live with other believers.

days.reflection:
Paul warns against attachment to money and calls for a generous life, trusting in God. He presents neither income as a measure of faithfulness, nor a lack of resources as a guarantee of wisdom. The passage invites us to examine our relationship with possessions.

A plan for a shared life requires talking about priorities: work, spending, savings, debts, generosity, and responsibilities toward family members. The goal of this conversation is to understand what will genuinely affect the household. Financial habits are often formed in different family contexts; they deserve to be explained before being judged.

You do not need to ask for every financial detail at a first meeting. As commitment becomes more serious, each person should be able to present honestly the realities that matter for a shared life. Privacy must still be respected, and no one acquires a right to control the other person's resources. Seek responsibility, clarity, and the ability to make decisions together, without making wealth a condition of personal worth.
days.practice: Choose two topics to prepare from among the following: spending, debts, work, generosity, and support for family members. Depending on the stage of the relationship, either propose an exchange or begin by clarifying your own habits.

discernment.reading: Observe the teaching addressed to those who desire to become wealthy and to those who already possess goods.
discernment.prayer: Father, you know my needs and my material anxieties. Free my heart from greed, comparison, and shame. Holy Spirit, teach me to manage what has been entrusted to me with honesty and generosity. Give me the courage to speak clearly about my responsibilities. If a relationship is moving forward, help us to understand our habits and to prepare realistic decisions, with respect for each person. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Present to God the first emotion that the subject of money stirs in you: fear, security, shame, or the desire for success. This emotion can help you understand your story; it does not have to direct your choices on its own.
questions: What priorities do my financial habits reveal?
What current responsibilities would affect a future shared life?
On what subject do we need a clearer conversation?
discernment.deeper: Read Hebrews 13:5–6 on the relationship to possessions and trust in God.

days.reflection:
Genesis presents a marital bond that commits two people to a new shared life. Proverbs speaks of a house established through wisdom and understanding. Together, these texts invite reflection on how to build a home, without providing a single model of organization for every family.

Before marriage, several subjects deserve to be addressed: where you will live, work, household responsibilities, relationships with extended family, the desire or lack thereof to have children, and convictions about how to raise them. Children or other dependents may already rely on one of you. Their reality must be welcomed honestly.

Honoring your family does not mean surrendering to them the decision to marry. Building a home does not require cutting ties with those close to you either. It is about being able to set boundaries and share responsibilities together. Some disagreements can be worked through; others touch on fundamental life plans. Discuss them without promising that the other person will change. The desire for children can be shared without any guarantee of fertility, and the absence of children takes nothing away from the dignity of a couple.
days.practice: Choose a subject that has not yet been much discussed: where you will live, household responsibilities, extended family, or children. Prepare a question that leaves the other person the freedom to express a wish that differs from your own.

discernment.reading: Consider the new unity of the couple and the image of a house built with wisdom.
discernment.prayer: Lord, I bring before you my family, my story, and the home I hope to build. Holy Spirit, give me the wisdom to honor those close to me while taking ownership of my own choices. Help me to speak about practical matters with gentleness and honesty. Make me attentive to those already entrusted to my care. Teach us to discern what can be built together and what requires genuine clarification. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: Bring before God a family habit you wish to keep and another you wish to transform. Receive your story with honesty, without believing you are condemned to repeat all of it.
questions: Which aspects of the daily life I desire have I already expressed, and which have I only imagined?
What family responsibilities need to be known and respected?
What difference in life plans would be difficult to live with if it remained unchanged?
discernment.deeper: Read Ephesians 6:1–4, paying attention to the responsibility of parents toward their children.

days.reflection:
Paul calls believers to a sexual conduct that reflects their belonging to God, without exploiting others. Within the Christian framework of this journey, sexual intimacy is reserved for marriage. This conviction calls for an honest conversation and personal accountability; it does not justify control or humiliation.

Your boundaries also concern the pace of the relationship, physical contact, messages, and intimate images. Affection gives no one the right to another person's body. A refusal must be respected, including within marriage. Pressure, manipulation, and persistence after a refusal are not proofs of love.

Your history does not reduce you to your mistakes or your wounds. If you have experienced assault, the fault is not yours. If you recognize choices you wish to change, you can seek God's forgiveness, compassionate support, and a new way of living. Do not pressure the other person to recount every detail of their past. Marriage does not replace the work of self-discipline and respect that begins today.
days.practice: Identify a concrete boundary you can put into practice. If expressing it directly puts you in danger, seek confidential support first; Day 25 provides reference points.

discernment.reading: Observe the connection between sanctification, self-discipline, and respect for the other person.
discernment.prayer: Father, thank you for the dignity you give to my body and my person. Holy Spirit, lead me into a life that honors you. Teach me to express my boundaries and to fully respect those of the other person. Heal what is wounded and give me the courage to seek the support I need. May affection never become a justification for exerting pressure. Grow within me the freedom to obey you with trust. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: Bring before God a boundary you wish to clarify. You may simply remain in prayer if returning to your story is too difficult today; no intimate details are required in this journal.
questions: What boundaries do I need to express clearly?
How is a refusal received — on my side and on the other person's side?
What support would help me live out my convictions without shame or isolation?
discernment.deeper: Read 1 Corinthians 6:19–20. Belonging to God does not give any suitor a right of possession over you.

days.reflection:
This word of wisdom cautions against moving forward hastily without understanding. It speaks to a common situation: several people express interest or make a proposal, and you feel pressured to choose. This day is addressed especially to women who receive multiple proposals, but the same principles apply to everyone.

Being approached creates no emotional debt. A gift, family support, a person's reputation, or a spiritual word does not obligate you to accept. You may ask for time, decline a proposal, or choose none of these relationships. The question remains: do you freely wish to get to know this person, and is there a genuine possibility of moving forward together?

It would be unjust to rank people as though they were competing offers, or to promise exclusivity to several people at once. Examine each situation for what it actually is: the intentions expressed, the known facts, your own availability, and the questions still unanswered. If you ask for more time, be clear about what you can and cannot promise. The other person remains free not to wait. A respectful response can be firm, without making humiliating comparisons or presenting your reasons as an unquestionable word from God.
days.practice: Prepare an honest response for a current situation. For example: "Thank you for your approach. I need time to think, and I cannot promise you a commitment." For a refusal: "I do not wish to pursue this relationship with a view to marriage." Adapt the wording to your own situation. If you are not currently receiving any proposals, write down the boundaries that would help you in this kind of situation.

discernment.reading: Notice the warning against haste that lacks knowledge.
discernment.prayer: Lord, I bring before you the proposals I am receiving and the emotions they stir in me. Holy Spirit, keep me from choosing under pressure, out of fear of missing an opportunity, or out of a need to be admired. Grant me the ability to regard each person with respect and to remain honest about my availability. Teach me to recognize what I truly want, to seek the information I need, and to say yes, wait, or no with freedom. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: Set aside for a moment the opinions and expectations of those around you. Before God, ask yourself what you can truthfully say today. An answer that is not yet complete can be expressed without giving the impression that a commitment has already been made.
questions: What proposals have actually been made, and how have I responded?
What comes from my own desire, and what comes from outside pressure?
What boundary or clarification do I need to communicate to someone involved?
discernment.deeper: Re-read Proverbs 19:2 and 1 Corinthians 7:39 keeping their contexts in mind. Neither the urgency of those around you nor a rare opportunity can replace an informed personal choice.

days.reflection:
These passages address relationships between believers. We apply them here to a specific situation: feeling interest in more than one person. This day speaks especially to men who hesitate between several possible relationships; its call to honesty applies to everyone.

Feeling attracted to someone is not a promise of marriage. It does not mean that a relationship exists or that the feeling is mutual. Kindness, a deep conversation, and friendship do not constitute consent to a romantic approach. Take time to distinguish between attraction, genuine knowledge of a person, and intentions that have actually been expressed.

You are not required to announce every passing attraction. You are, however, responsible for the expectations your words and actions create. Avoid giving several people the impression that each of them is the only one in an exclusive relationship. If you have already made a commitment, honestly clarify that situation before pursuing another relationship. No method of prayer can turn indecision into permission to keep others in ambiguity. You may step back to understand your own motivations, while respecting each person's freedom to withdraw.
days.practice: Choose one course of action: stop an ambiguous behavior, clarify your intentions within an actual relationship, or step back before moving forward. If you are not in this situation, reflect on how you would distinguish a friendship from a romantic approach.

discernment.reading: Notice the attention given to the good of others and to truth in community life.
discernment.prayer: Father, I bring before you my attractions and my hesitations. Holy Spirit, help me to see people with respect, beyond what they offer me. Show me the expectations I may have fostered without clarity. Give me the courage to correct my words, to honor my commitments, and to accept that an interest may not be shared. Teach me to move forward with sincerity and to let go of what only feeds my need for attention. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: Ask God to show you what falls within your responsibility: a word to correct, an ambiguous behavior to stop, or a question to ask. Do not try to guess inwardly what the other person feels; those feelings belong to them and must be allowed to be expressed freely.
questions: Which interests are mutual and openly expressed, and which are merely assumed?
Have my actions led anyone to believe in a commitment I am not actually making?
What honest step would honor the people involved today?
discernment.deeper: Read Romans 13:8–10 on a way of loving that is attentive to the good of others.

days.theme: Checking Whether a Vision Is Shared
days.reflection:
Paul calls believers to sincere affection and mutual honor. This command does not ask you to feel romantic love for someone, nor to accept a proposal. Its application to discernment consists in treating the other person with truth.

This week has raised subjects that are sometimes decisive: faith, responsibilities, everyday life, boundaries, and intentions. A shared vision cannot rest solely on what you hope for or on what those around you approve. It requires that both people freely express their desire to move forward and that they understand the step being considered.

It may be too early to speak of marriage while still being appropriate to get to know one another. It may also become clear that one of the two does not wish to continue. Acknowledging this reality is a way of honoring the other person. If no one currently shares such a vision with you, this week remains useful for clarifying your direction and your habits. You do not need to invent a relationship in order to complete this journey successfully.
days.practice: Choose one single useful clarification. If a relationship exists, suggest a time to speak freely about it. If not, note a personal area of growth and a friendship or community relationship to cultivate.

discernment.reading: Identify the call to sincerity and respect in brotherly love.
discernment.prayer: Lord, thank You for what is becoming clearer and for what remains to be learned. Holy Spirit, help me to receive the truth about a relationship, even when it differs from my hope. Grant me the grace to respect the intentions and the pace of the other person without losing my own freedom. If a shared vision is being built, strengthen our sincerity. If our paths do not come together, accompany me through letting go and into the rest of my life. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: Bring before God one reality you accept easily and another that costs you something. You may entrust your disappointment to Him without turning it into a reproach against the other person or a sign that God has abandoned you.
questions: What has each of us expressed about the future of this relationship?
What agreement is real, and what difference still matters?
What step corresponds today to our mutual consent and knowledge of one another?
discernment.deeper: Return to your notes from days 15 to 20. Distinguish what is shared, what remains to be discussed, and what already constitutes a significant disagreement. No scoring or ranking of persons is necessary.

days.reflection:
Paul calls the community to welcome the work of the Spirit while also examining what is presented as prophetic. John calls for testing the spirits in the face of false prophets, paying particular attention to their confession of Jesus Christ. These texts call for an openness to God accompanied by vigilance; they do not describe a technique for identifying a spouse.

You may ask the Holy Spirit to guide you and receive with gratitude what you believe you are given in prayer. Then distinguish the experience from your interpretation of it: a thought, a dream, a conviction, or a word received does not automatically explain itself. An unusual encounter or a repeated word is not sufficient to establish that God is calling you to marry.

Examine what is being proposed in the light of Scripture in its context. Bring it to mature believers, consider the facts, and allow time to shed light on the situation. Agreement with a biblical principle is necessary, but does not by itself prove the divine origin of a specific impression. A direction you believe you have received cannot bind another person's conscience in your place. Their refusal must be respected. You may revise an interpretation without abandoning a sincere pursuit of the Spirit's guidance. Re-read 1 Thessalonians 5 if needed.
days.practice: If there is one, choose an important impression in your discernment. Note what still needs to be examined and identify a mature person to speak with about it. Do not invent a spiritual experience in order to fill this day.

discernment.reading: Observe how welcoming the work of the Spirit is accompanied by discernment.
discernment.prayer: Holy Spirit, I desire to receive Your guidance with a humble heart. Enlighten my understanding and teach me to test what I believe I receive. Keep me from closing my heart to Your work, and equally from presenting my own preferences under Your authority. If I have misunderstood, give me the freedom to acknowledge it. May Your Word govern my judgment, and may my words always respect the freedom of the other person. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: Remain for a few moments in openness before God. If an impression comes, note separately what you experienced and the meaning you attribute to it. If nothing particular comes, continue with confidence in what the Word is already inviting you to practice.
questions: What did I actually perceive or hear, and what did I conclude from it?
Does this interpretation hold up against biblical reading, the facts, and wise counsel?
Am I prepared to acknowledge an error and to respect the other person's freedom?
discernment.deeper: Re-read the context of 1 John 4:1–6. The question of the identity of Christ is central there; this passage cannot be reduced to the evaluation of a romantic feeling.

days.reflection:
James contrasts conduct driven by rivalry with a wisdom that shows itself in gentleness, uprightness, and concern for peace. His letter examines community life and the ambitions of those who claim to know. For our discernment, it invites us to look at the way we seek an answer just as much as at the answer we desire.

How do you react when advice contradicts you? Do you accept that the other person has their own pace and their own will? Do you seek to understand, or to win the agreement of those around you? A wise approach makes room for truth, for correction, and for the good of the people involved. You can make a firm decision while still remaining humble.

The peace spoken of here should not become a test for the absence of unpleasant emotion. A right decision can be accompanied by sadness or fear; an unwise choice can bring immediate relief. Ask God for a wisdom that is recognized in your actions, then consider together the Word, the facts, counsel, and each person's freedom. You may read the full chapter to continue your meditation.
days.practice: Return to a conclusion you considered obvious. Write down the fact that supports it, what might correct it, and what you can do to move forward with integrity.

discernment.reading: Observe the attitudes associated with the two ways of seeking wisdom.
discernment.prayer: Father, give me a wisdom that shows itself in my conduct. Holy Spirit, reveal to me the jealousy, ambition, or desire to be right whenever they are steering my decisions. Teach me to receive correction without closing myself off. Give me a desire to seek peace with truth and to treat people with gentleness. When I must make a difficult decision, sustain my courage and keep my heart humble. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Bring before God a disagreement with someone close to you, or a piece of advice that unsettled you. Look for what you can examine honestly, without feeling obligated to accept everything you were told.
questions: What attitude is accompanying my search for an answer right now?
How did I react to information that went against what I wanted?
What action would express humble and attentive wisdom today?
discernment.deeper: Return to James 1:5 and the notes from day 1. Observe how your way of asking for wisdom has developed.

days.theme: Receiving counsel without surrendering my responsibility
days.reflection:
This proverb underlines the value of seeking counsel. It does not promise that a group will always give the right answer, and it does not transfer your choice to a spiritual leader or to your family. Counsel helps you see what you cannot perceive on your own.

Choose mature people who are able to listen to the facts, respect confidentiality, and acknowledge their own limits. An independent perspective is particularly valuable when someone close to you strongly wants a marriage to happen. One person who knows your life may notice a recurring pattern; another may help you examine a biblical question. Their observations can complement one another without becoming a majority vote.

Also bring forward what is troubling you. If you share only the favorable elements, you prevent the counsel from bearing on the real situation. Avoid, however, seeking one opinion after another until you receive the answer you want. The goal is to learn and to reflect before God. A word that imposes marriage, makes threats, or demands unlimited access to your life must not be received as unquestionable authority. When safety is at stake, specialized support may be necessary.
days.practice: Prepare a brief summary: three relevant facts, two questions, and the kind of help you are looking for. You can then seek a conversation yourself, sharing only the information that is necessary.

discernment.reading: Consider the help that several different perspectives can bring to the preparation of an important decision.
discernment.prayer: Lord, thank you for the people through whom you can bring me light and encouragement. Holy Spirit, guide me toward counsel that is wise, honest, and respectful. Give me the humility to present the facts without shaping them to suit me. Teach me to listen, to test what I hear, and to keep hold of my own responsibility. May I seek neither easy approval nor someone who will decide in my place. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Think of a person with whom you could speak freely. Bring before God what reassures you and what holds you back. You may choose a different person to speak with if confidentiality or freedom are not being respected.
questions: Who can listen to me with maturity, discretion, and independence?
What important fact do I tend to leave out when I seek counsel?
What piece of counsel I have received deserves to be explored further or examined in light of Scripture?
discernment.deeper: Read Proverbs 12:15 and 19:20. Openness to counsel goes hand in hand with patient learning.

days.reflection:
Christian love does not ask us to conceal harm in order to preserve the image of a relationship. These passages address the conduct of believers; we apply them here to what undermines dignity and safety in a relationship.

Threats, humiliation, enforced surveillance, and forced sexual acts must be taken seriously. Promises made after a violent episode do not cancel what happened. You are not responsible for the violence another person inflicts. You can seek confidential support from a trusted person and a specialist service. If you are in immediate danger, contact the emergency services in your country as soon as you can do so safely.

A religious claim cannot justify domination. Forgiving does not mean restoring access to yourself, continuing the relationship, or preparing for marriage. You do not have to confront the person alone in order to have the right to protect yourself. A spiritual approach can accompany the search for help; it does not replace it.

If you recognize controlling or violent behavior in yourself, take responsibility for it, stop the pressure, and seek specialized help to change. Do not demand immediate forgiveness or a resumption of the relationship. The freedom and safety of the other person must be respected.
days.practice: Identify a person or service that can help you safely. If this concerns you, choose your next protective step with appropriate support; you do not have to wait until the end of this journey.

discernment.reading: Notice the call to reject evil and to take no part in it.
discernment.prayer: God of justice and compassion, shed light on what needs to be named in my situation. Holy Spirit, give me the courage to seek the help I need and not to cover over harm with religious language. Surround those who are hurting with safe support. Where I have caused harm, lead me to take responsibility for it without excuse or pressure on the other person. Teach me to hold together truth, protection, and hope. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: You can simply remain before God without reliving or recounting painful events in detail. Seeking concrete help may be the right step for today; do not wait for a spiritual impression before protecting yourself.
questions: Can I say no and seek help without fearing retaliation?
What behavior have I minimized, endured, or inflicted?
What confidential and safe support can I reach out to?
discernment.journalNote: You may respond aloud, skip these questions, or keep nothing in writing if your notes could be seen by someone else.
discernment.deeper: Look for a specialist service suited to your country and situation. This practical reading can wait if immediate help is needed.

days.reflection:
These words of wisdom invite us to listen and to verify what we think we know. They do not ask us to become suspicious of everyone. They encourage careful judgment that is attentive to the information available and to its limits.

At this stage, questions may remain about faith, responsibilities, intentions, or conduct that concerns you. Some can receive an answer through conversation. Others require time to observe consistency. There are also disagreements that are already known and that it would be misleading to present as mere unknowns. Ask yourself whether you were waiting for information or whether you were mainly waiting for the other person to become different.

Clarification must respect privacy and the stage of the relationship. It does not authorize surveillance or demanding access to someone's devices. Conversely, you do not have to resolve every doubt in order to have the right to decline a commitment. One significant piece of information that remains inaccessible can be enough to justify a pause. In the presence of fear or violence, the safety guidelines from Day 25 take precedence over this conversational approach.
days.practice: Complete four elements: the specific question, how to shed light on it, the person involved, and an appropriate moment to revisit it. This moment organizes your reflection; it does not set a mandatory date to say yes.

discernment.reading: Notice the importance of understanding before drawing conclusions from only one account.
discernment.prayer: Father, I entrust to you the questions that remain open. Holy Spirit, help me to discern which ones call for conversation, which need time, and which require a decision. Keep me from interpreting too quickly and from endlessly postponing what is already clear. Give me the patience to know without controlling, and the freedom to acknowledge the limits of what I can know today. In the name of Jesus, amen.
discernment.listening: Choose a single question and bring it before God. Ask for one realistic next step. You may acknowledge that you do not yet have enough information to move forward.
questions: Which open question could genuinely change my next step?
Is this an unknown, a known disagreement, or the hope that something will change?
How can I clarify it in a way that is respectful and safe?
discernment.deeper: Read Proverbs 14:15. Prudence invites us to consider our path, without seeking absolute certainty about the entire future.

days.reflection:
Paul speaks of the life of the body of Christ. Truth expressed in love contributes to relationships that can grow. In loving discernment, this orientation helps us move out of an ambiguity that has become unnecessary or misleading.

You may want to get to know someone better without being ready to speak of marriage. You may ask for time on a specific question. You may also not wish to continue. A clear word indicates what you want, what you are not promising, and, if necessary, what remains to be discussed. It allows the other person to respond freely.

You do not have to present every decision as a certain instruction from God for it to deserve respect. You can explain that you have prayed and reflected, and then own your response. Avoid comparisons with other people and phrases that give false hope. Kindness does not require endless justification. If a response is given to you, also receive the other person's right to choose. When a direct conversation poses a danger, choose a safe means of communication with appropriate support.
days.practice: Write a short statement, with no obligation to send it today. For example: "I would like to keep getting to know you, without yet making a promise of marriage"; "I need to clarify this point before moving forward"; or "I do not wish to continue this romantic relationship." Adapt it to what is true and to your safety.

discernment.reading: Observe how truth is woven into growth and into relationship with others.
discernment.prayer: Lord, give me words that are honest and kind. Holy Spirit, help me to say what I can genuinely stand behind. Keep me from promises made only to avoid immediate disappointment, and from explanations that humiliate. Give me the courage to bring clarity and the humility to receive the other person's response. May my spiritual language serve the truth and never become a form of pressure. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Bring to God the conversation you are dreading. Ask him to help you distinguish between the hurt you cannot entirely prevent and the harm you can avoid through a truthful word.
questions: What response can I honestly give at this stage?
Does the way I have worded things suggest a promise I am not making?
How can I respect the freedom and dignity of the other person?
discernment.deeper: Read Colossians 4:6 on speech that is attentive to the person being addressed.

days.theme: Entrusting the Next Step to God
days.reflection:
This passage invites us to acknowledge God in our path and not to make our own judgment the sole authority. It does not promise detailed knowledge of the future. For discernment, it teaches us to keep praying, learning, and acting under God's guidance.

Look back over your journey. What have you understood from Scripture? What has changed in your motivations, in the way you have come to know the other person, or in speaking truthfully? What facts, conversations, and counsel have shed light on your situation? You do not need to have received an extraordinary experience or to have chosen a spouse in order to recognize fruit from these days.

The next step can take four forms: continuing to get to know each other; considering marriage preparation together when your intention is clear; waiting or taking a pause to gain clarity; stepping back from a relationship. None of these outcomes is determined by the number of days completed. Marriage preparation continues to examine the plan freely and does not constitute consent already given to the ceremony.

If no relationship is in view, continue your life with God, your friendships, and your responsibilities. You can hold your desire for marriage without putting your whole life on hold until it is fulfilled. Faithfulness to God is also lived out in the next ordinary step.
days.practice: Complete the review below, then choose one single actionable step. If a relationship exists, distinguish your personal desire from what you have both expressed. Any shared step requires your mutual consent.

discernment.reading: Observe the place of trust in God in the ordering of life.
discernment.prayer: Father, thank you for accompanying me through these days. I place before you what I have understood and what remains uncertain. Holy Spirit, guide my next step in faithfulness to your Word. Give me the courage to move forward when that is wise, the patience to wait, and the freedom to step back when that is necessary. Bless the people involved and help me to respect their path. May my trust remain in you, whatever the outcome of this relationship. In Jesus' name, amen.
discernment.listening: Remain for a moment in gratitude. Do not try at all costs to obtain a final confirmation. You can entrust your decision to God and continue to examine it with humility.
questions: What has become clear enough to take a next step?
What remains to be understood or worked through, personally or together?
What step will I take, with what support and at what pace?
discernment.deeper: Return to a passage or a resource that helped you. You can continue in prayer and conversation beyond these 28 days.
discernment.review:
What Scripture has taught or reminded me

An attitude in which I want to keep growing

The facts that shed light on my current situation

My personal desire, distinct from the other person's

What we have both freely expressed, if a relationship exists

An important question that remains open

A boundary I need to respect or to have respected

Helpful counsel I have received, and what I am taking from it

My next concrete step

The support and the moment that will help me to reassess

Continuing to get to know each other: We both want to know each other better, with clear intentions and boundaries, and without a premature promise of marriage.

Considering marriage preparation: We are freely expressing a shared intention and wish to explore it further with appropriate accompaniment. Important questions continue to be examined.

Waiting or taking a pause: A question, a disagreement, or our availability requires time. We clarify what this waiting means; no one is obligated to wait indefinitely.

Stepping back from the relationship: I do not wish to continue, or the other person does not. The response is respected, without spiritual pressure or any attempt to force a change of mind.
